title: New Zealand Formally Makes English an Official Language, Drawing Ridicule at Home
excerpt: Parliament passed the English Language Bill despite widespread criticism that the move was unnecessary in a country where 95% of the population already speaks the language.
body:
• New Zealand's parliament passed the English Language Bill on July 30, making English a de jure official language alongside Maori and New Zealand Sign Language
  • The bill was part of a coalition agreement between the National Party and New Zealand First, which campaigned on formalizing English's status
  • Nearly two-thirds of 1,601 public submissions opposed the legislation, with critics calling it unnecessary and potentially undermining indigenous language protections
  • More than 95% of New Zealand's population already speaks English; the bill introduces no new rules or rights for the language

New Zealand has formally made English one of its official languages — a move that has drawn more mockery than celebration in a country where the language has been dominant for over 160 years.

The English Language Bill cleared its third and final reading in the House of Representatives on July 30, giving English the same de jure status as Maori and New Zealand Sign Language. The legislation, introduced by the ruling National-led coalition government in February, codifies what has long been assumed: that English is the working language of New Zealand's courts, parliament, and government agencies.

A Coalition Promise Fulfilled

The bill originated as a campaign pledge by the nationalist New Zealand First party during the 2023 general election. Following coalition negotiations, National agreed to pass legislation designating English as an official language as part of the coalition agreement with New Zealand First and the ACT party.

Casey Costello, a New Zealand First MP, defended the move during the third reading debate. "The purpose of this short, straightforward bill is to recognize in legislation what has long been assumed in New Zealand — namely, that English is an official language of our country," she told parliament, adding that it was "not trivial, unnecessary, or a distraction."

The bill's text is notably modest. It states that the addition of English as an official language will not require any new rules for it to continue being used in legal, political, and government settings — an acknowledgment that the legislation changes virtually nothing in practice.

Widespread Ridicule and Opposition

The bill provoked sharp criticism from opposition lawmakers and the public alike. A speech by Green Party MP Tamatha Paul during the third reading was viewed more than six million times on Instagram, in which she condemned the legislation as a waste of time and accused the government of being "snowflakes" who "see te reo Maori and they shiver in their boots."

"We had to march our asses to parliament demanding that the indigenous first language of this country be recognized and not beaten out of the mouths of its native speakers."

— Tamatha Paul, Green Party MP

Paul pointed out that English is not even a formal official language in England itself. Labour MP Camilla Belich offered her own barb during the debate, musing aloud whether the government "might want to legislate for the changing of the seasons."

The country's Justice Committee received written submissions from 1,601 people and groups, with almost two-thirds opposing the bill. Critics argued it was an unnecessary use of resources, would create social division, and risked undermining the statutory protections that Maori and NZ Sign Language received precisely because they needed legislative support to survive.

Context and Significance

English has been the dominant language in New Zealand since British settlers became the majority population in the 1860s. According to 2023 government data, more than 95% of the population — nearly 4.8 million people — speak English, compared to just 4.3% who speak Maori and 0.5% who use sign language.

Maori was made an official language in 1987 following decades of suppression during the colonial era, while NZ Sign Language gained official status in 2006. The Labour Party, which voted for the bill despite reservations, noted that legislation for those languages "was and is necessary to recognize both of these important and significant languages that are still only used by a minority of the population. English does not need the same support to ensure its survival."

New Zealand joins only a handful of English-speaking nations that have formally codified the language's status. The United Kingdom, Australia, and the United States do not have English as a de jure official language.

What's Next

The bill awaits Royal Assent from Governor-General Cindy Kiro before becoming law. While the legislation itself introduces no practical changes, it has reignited debates about the place of Maori language and culture in New Zealand's national identity — questions that resonate well beyond Wellington's parliamentary chambers.
